seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 556 HTS Chapter 44 wood lines: most are Free or under 11% at base; softwood logs and lumber pay the 10% Section 232 duty, Canadian lumber also AD/CVD (35.19% for most mills), Canadian plywood and hardwood 50% Section 338, China 25% Section 301.

overview.intro:
Chapter 44 covers wood: fuel wood, chips and pellets (4401), charcoal (4402), logs (4403), sawn lumber (4407), veneer (4408), mouldings and flooring strips (4409), panels such as particle board and OSB (4410), fiberboard and MDF (4411) and plywood (4412), and articles of wood: frames, pallets and crates, barrels, tool handles, doors, windows, engineered flooring and other builders' joinery (4418), kitchenware, ornaments and other articles. Furniture and wooden cabinets are in Chapter 94. The base rates are low: **356 of 556 lines are Free**, and the rest pay 1.5% to 10.7%, with plywood at up to 8%.

Three things decide the cost. **Section 232 (timber and lumber)** charges **10%** on softwood logs, sleepers and sawn lumber (106 lines, heading 9903.76.01) from every country since October 14, 2025; FTA claims do not reduce it. **Canada's Section 338 duty** adds **50%** to 154 other Canadian wood lines, including plywood, hardwood lumber, veneer, MDF, mouldings and windows, even with USMCA. And Chinese wood pays **25% Section 301** (List 3) plus 12.5% on most non-Section 232 lines.

On top of the tariff, **Canadian softwood lumber carries antidumping and countervailing duties** (35.19% for most producers), and hardwood plywood, multilayered flooring and mouldings from China, and hardwood plywood from Indonesia and Vietnam are under AD/CVD orders or new findings. These are company-specific and not part of this table or the calculator; see Tariff updates and Import documents.

stats.label: Section 232 (timber & lumber)
stats.note: 10% on softwood logs, sleepers and sawn lumber (9903.76.01), all countries

productGroups.label: Fuel wood, chips, pellets & sawdust
productGroups.blurb: Firewood, wood chips and particles, sawdust, wood pellets and briquettes: 13 lines, all Free. Outside Section 232; most countries pay the 2026 Section 301 duty, China 37.5%. Canadian non-coniferous chips pay Section 338.

productGroups.label: Wood charcoal
productGroups.blurb: Charcoal including shell or nut charcoal and briquettes: 3 lines, Free. Outside Section 232; Canadian charcoal (4402.90) pays the 50% Section 338 duty.

productGroups.label: Logs (wood in the rough)
productGroups.blurb: Logs and poles, coniferous and hardwood, treated or not: 85 lines, all Free. Softwood logs (pine, fir, spruce and other conifers, 62 lines) pay the 10% Section 232 duty; hardwood and tropical logs do not.

productGroups.label: Hoopwood, split poles & stakes
productGroups.blurb: Hoopwood, split poles, piles, pickets and stakes, chipwood: 6 lines, Free. Outside Section 232.

productGroups.label: Wood wool & wood flour
productGroups.blurb: Wood wool (excelsior) and wood flour: 1 line at 3.2%.

productGroups.label: Railway sleepers (cross-ties)
productGroups.blurb: Railway or tramway sleepers of wood: 4 lines, Free. Coniferous sleepers pay the 10% Section 232 duty.

productGroups.label: Sawn lumber (softwood & hardwood)
productGroups.blurb: Wood sawn or chipped lengthwise, over 6 mm thick: 74 lines, all Free. Softwood lumber (pine, fir, spruce, S-P-F, hem-fir and other conifers, 42 lines) pays 10% Section 232 from every country; Canadian softwood lumber also carries AD/CVD. Hardwood and tropical lumber are outside Section 232. The largest import group (≈$7.4B in 2025).

productGroups.label: Veneer sheets
productGroups.blurb: Sheets for veneering and plywood, 6 mm or less: 27 lines, Free. Canadian coniferous veneer pays Section 338.

productGroups.label: Mouldings, flooring strips & profiled wood
productGroups.blurb: Wood continuously shaped (tongued, grooved, moulded) along any edge or face, including solid flooring strips: 47 lines, Free to 4.9%. Chinese mouldings and millwork carry AD/CVD; many Canadian pine and other mouldings pay Section 338.

productGroups.label: Particle board & OSB
productGroups.blurb: Particle board, oriented strand board (OSB) and similar board: 11 lines, Free. Outside Section 232; Canadian OSB is Free with USMCA, other Canadian boards (4410.19) pay Section 338.

productGroups.label: Fiberboard & MDF
productGroups.blurb: Medium-density fiberboard (MDF), hardboard and other fiberboard: 36 lines, Free to 6% (some 1.9¢/kg + 1.5%). Canadian MDF of 4411.13–4411.14 pays Section 338.

productGroups.label: Plywood & laminated wood
productGroups.blurb: Plywood, veneered panels, LVL and similar laminated wood: 123 lines, Free to 8%. Canadian plywood pays the 50% Section 338 duty. Hardwood plywood from China is under AD/CVD orders, and the ITC found injury from hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam in September 2026.

productGroups.label: Densified wood
productGroups.blurb: Densified wood in blocks, plates, strips or profile shapes: 1 line at 3.7%; Canadian goods pay Section 338.

productGroups.label: Wooden frames
productGroups.blurb: Frames for paintings, photographs and mirrors: 2 lines at 3.9%. Chinese frames are on Section 301 List 4A (7.5%).

productGroups.label: Pallets, crates & cable drums
productGroups.blurb: Packing cases, boxes, crates, cable drums and pallets: 5 lines, Free or 10.7%. Wood packaging must meet the ISPM 15 treatment rules.

productGroups.label: Casks, barrels & staves
productGroups.blurb: Barrels, casks, vats and their parts, including staves: 10 lines, Free or 3.2%.

productGroups.label: Tools, handles & shoe lasts
productGroups.blurb: Tool bodies, tool handles, broom and brush bodies, boot and shoe lasts: 5 lines, Free or 5.1%.

productGroups.label: Doors, windows, flooring & builders' joinery
productGroups.blurb: Windows, doors and frames, formwork, shingles and shakes, posts and beams, glulam and CLT, assembled and engineered flooring panels: 45 lines, Free to 8%. Canadian windows pay Section 338; Chinese multilayered flooring carries AD/CVD.

productGroups.label: Wooden tableware & kitchenware
productGroups.blurb: Cutting boards, bowls, chopsticks and other tableware of wood and bamboo: 8 lines, 3.2% or 5.3%. Not on China's Section 301 lists except two lines.

productGroups.label: Ornaments, marquetry & wooden boxes
productGroups.blurb: Statuettes and ornaments, marquetry, jewelry and cutlery boxes and small wooden furnishings: 8 lines, Free to 4.3%.

productGroups.label: Other articles of wood
productGroups.blurb: Clothes hangers, clothespins, toothpicks, dowels, matchsticks, coffins, pencil slats, pet gates and other articles: 42 lines, Free to 10.7%.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: $500,000 of S-P-F softwood lumber from Canada
workedExamples.body: S-P-F lumber is **Free**, but it is a Section 232 softwood lumber article, so it pays **+10%** (9903.76.01): **$50,000**, with or without a USMCA certification. On top come the **softwood lumber AD/CVD cash deposits**: 35.19% for most Canadian producers (20.56% AD + 14.63% CVD from the 2023 reviews), about **$175,950**. Section 338 does not apply to softwood lumber.

workedExamples.title: Hardwood plywood from Canada
workedExamples.body: Base **8%**, Free under USMCA, but Canadian plywood is on the note 51(b)(3) list, so it pays **+50%** Section 338 (9903.03.14) even with USMCA: **50%**, or **68%** without a USMCA claim (8% base + 50% + the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty, which is lifted only for USMCA goods). Plywood is not a Section 232 article.

workedExamples.title: OSB from Canada
workedExamples.body: Oriented strand board is **Free**, is not a Section 232 article and is not on the Section 338 list, so Canadian OSB with a USMCA certification pays **no duty**. Without the claim it pays 10% under the 2026 Section 301 action on Canada (9903.05.29).

workedExamples.title: Pine lumber from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Brazilian pine lumber is **Free** at base and pays only the **10%** Section 232 duty: goods under 9903.76.01 do not pay the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty or the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (notes 50(a)(vi)(4), 52(f)(4)). Brazilian pine **plywood** (4412.39.40, 8%) is not covered by Section 232 and pays 8% + 25% + 12.5% = **45.5%**.

workedExamples.title: Bamboo plywood from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Base **8%** plus **12.5%** under the 2026 Section 301 action on Vietnam (9903.05.84): **20.5%**. Hardwood and decorative plywood from Vietnam also faces the new AD/CVD case: Commerce made final affirmative findings in July 2026 and the ITC found injury on September 9, 2026; check the order and cash-deposit status before importing.

workedExamples.title: Wood pellets from Germany
workedExamples.body: Wood pellets are **Free** and outside Section 232. Under the 2026 Section 301 action the EU rate is **10% in place of the base rate** when the base rate is lower (9903.05.39), so EU pellets pay **10%**.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1** excludes, among others, wood chips and powders for perfumery or pharmacy (1211), plaiting bamboo (1401), activated charcoal (3802), goods of Chapter 46, footwear parts, machine parts and cases (Section XVI–XVII), clock cases and musical instruments, **furniture, lighting and prefabricated buildings (Chapter 94)**, toys and sports equipment (Chapter 95), pencils and other Chapter 96 articles (except brush and broom bodies and handles of wood) and works of art.

**Note 2** defines *densified wood*; **note 3** applies headings 4414–4421 to articles of particle board, fiberboard, laminated or densified wood; **note 4** lets products of 4410–4412 be worked to the shapes of 4409, curved, perforated or cut without leaving their heading; **note 6** extends "wood" to bamboo and other woody materials.

**Subheading notes:** *wood pellets* (4401.31: cylindrical, diameter up to 25 mm, length up to 100 mm, binder up to 3%) and *wood briquettes* (4401.32: minimum cross-section over 25 mm); *S-P-F* (4407.13) is wood from mixed stands of spruce, pine and fir, and *Hem-fir* (4407.14) from mixed stands of western hemlock and fir, in unknown proportions.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** Defines *wood waste*, *standard wood moldings* and *surface covered* (for 4411 and 4412: treated with preservatives, fillers, stains, paints or overlaid with paper, plastics or other material).

**2.** Sawed lumber and timbers, wooden utility poles and bundles of shingles (other than red cedar) need not be marked with the country of origin.

**3.** Heading 4409 includes articles with a repeating design worked along any edge or face.

**4.** Heading 4418 includes drilled or notched lumber studs and multi-layer assembled flooring panels with a face ply 4 mm or more thick.

A statistical note defines *rough* lumber for heading 4407 (edged, resawn, crosscut or trimmed, but not planed or end- or edge-glued).

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 44: Wood and Articles of Wood; Wood Charcoal — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Lumber & Wood Tariff Updates 2025–2026: 10% Section 232, Canada Section 338, Softwood AD/CVD (HTS Ch. 44) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every U.S. tariff change on lumber and wood products since 2025 with Federal Register citations: the 10% Section 232 duty on softwood lumber (October 2025), Canada's 50% Section 338 duty on plywood and hardwood (August 2026), the 2026 Section 301 actions, the end of the IEEPA duties, and the softwood lumber and plywood AD/CVD cases.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule, the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026), and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 44 today. Base rates did not change; one statistical line was added (4420.19.00.00).

The extra duties changed a lot. Proclamation 10976 put a **10% Section 232 duty on softwood timber and lumber** from every country on **October 14, 2025** (with 25% on upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets in Chapter 94). The IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026** and the Section 122 surcharge on July 23, 2026. In July 2026 the **2026 Section 301 actions** (10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies) and the **25% Brazil duty** took effect on most non-Section 232 wood lines, and on **August 22, 2026** Canada's **50% Section 338 duty** reached 154 lines of Canadian plywood, hardwood lumber, veneer, MDF, mouldings, windows and other wood products, USMCA or not.

Antidumping and countervailing duties on **Canadian softwood lumber** (35.19% for most producers since the 2023 reviews) and on Chinese hardwood plywood, flooring and mouldings, and the new **hardwood and decorative plywood** case on China, Indonesia and Vietnam, are listed for reference and **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 44 from any country: Section 232 timber and lumber (note 37), Canada Section 338 (note 51), China Section 301 (note 20), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies with their exemption and partner exception lists (notes 52(b), (c), (j)) and the Brazil duty (note 50), Russia's 35% in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. The main antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Chapter 44 products are listed for reference; the calculator does not model them. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.country: All countries (Canada, Brazil, Germany, Sweden, Chile, New Zealand and every other supplier)
inEffect.exemption: Covers softwood (coniferous) timber and lumber only (note 37(a)–(b)): coniferous logs and poles (4403.11, 4403.21–4403.26, 4403.99), coniferous sleepers (4406.11, 4406.91) and sawn softwood lumber (4407.11–4407.19, including S-P-F and hem-fir). Hardwood and tropical logs and lumber, plywood, OSB, MDF, mouldings, flooring and other articles of Chapter 44 are not covered. No country exemptions: Canada and Mexico pay it with USMCA, and it is collected on top of any FTA rate. For the UK the duty may not exceed 10%, and for the EU and Japan the total may not exceed 15% (clause 7), which the 10% on Free lumber already meets. Goods under 9903.76.01 do not pay the 2026 Section 301 or Brazil duties (notes 52(f)(4), 50(a)(vi)(4)). The 25%→30% and 25%→50% steps of Proclamations 10976 and 11000 apply to upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets (Chapter 94), not to lumber.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Softwood lumber costs 10% more from every country: $1,000,000 of Canadian or Swedish studs pays $100,000, plus any AD/CVD for Canadian lumber.

inEffect.exemption: Note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14, Proclamation 11048) lists 148 Chapter 44 lines: nearly all plywood and laminated wood (4412), non-coniferous fuel wood (4401.12), other charcoal (4402.90), hardwood lumber nesoi (4407.99), coniferous veneer (4408.10), pine and other mouldings (4409.10.40, 4409.10.50, 4409.10.90, 4409.29.91), other board (4410.19), MDF (4411.13, 4411.14), windows (4418.21, 4418.29), frames (4414.90), ornaments (4420.19) and some other articles (4421.99). Note 51(b)(1) (9903.03.12, Proclamation 11046) adds 6 lines: densified wood, some kitchenware, marquetry and other articles. Charged even when USMCA is claimed (the headings' Special column is "+ 50%"). Softwood lumber, logs, OSB, particle board and most flooring are not on the lists. The start moved from August 19 to August 22, 2026 (Proclamation 11056); Proclamations 11064 and 11065 adjusted the lists from September 15, 2026. Canadian goods also pay the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.29) unless USMCA is claimed.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Canadian plywood, MDF, hardwood lumber and windows cost half their value again in duty: $200,000 of Canadian plywood pays $100,000.

inEffect.exemption: List 3 (9903.88.03, 25%) covers 518 Chapter 44 lines, nearly everything except most wooden tableware (4419), some ornaments and some other articles. List 4A (9903.88.15, 7.5%) covers frames (4414), a few kitchenware, marquetry and other articles. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China (9903.05.31) applies to the lines that are neither Section 232 lumber (note 52(f)(4)) nor on the note 52(b) exemption list (tropical logs, lumber and veneer). The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026. USTR confirmed on October 7, 2026 that the 2018 actions continue during the four-year review.

inEffect.exemption: Does not apply to Section 232 softwood lumber (note 52(f)(4)). Note 52(c) exempts one named eucalyptus plywood product. USMCA-qualifying goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.detail: 555 of 556 Chapter 44 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. One statistical line was added, 4420.19.00.00 (statuettes and ornaments of non-tropical wood), at the unchanged 3.2%.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 44 line, including on top of the 10% Section 232 duty on softwood lumber. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: ITC: injury from hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam
changes.detail: The ITC found that imports of hardwood and decorative plywood (excluding softwood structural plywood) from China, Indonesia and Vietnam injure the U.S. industry, after Commerce's final affirmative dumping and subsidy findings of July 21, 2026. The case covers 35 plywood subheadings of 4412 (including bamboo plywood 4412.10.05). The ITC terminated the cases on softwood structural plywood as negligible. Commerce issues the antidumping and countervailing duty orders after the ITC vote; they had not appeared in the Federal Register as of October 12, 2026.

changes.title: Section 338 duty on Canadian plywood, hardwood, MDF and windows
changes.detail: Proclamations 11046 and 11048 put a 50% duty on products of Canada in the note 51(b)(1) and 51(b)(3) lists (9903.03.12, 9903.03.14), charged even on USMCA goods. In Chapter 44 they reach 154 lines: nearly all plywood, hardwood lumber nesoi, coniferous veneer, mouldings, other board, MDF, windows, frames and some articles. Softwood lumber, logs, OSB and particle board are not listed. The start moved from August 19 to August 22, 2026 (Proclamation 11056), and Proclamations 11064 and 11065 adjusted the lists from September 15, 2026.

changes.title: Softwood lumber CVD order reinstated for D&G/Portbec
changes.detail: After a final Court of International Trade judgment, Commerce recalculated a 1.05% subsidy rate for Les Produits Forestiers D&G and Portbec, so their Canadian softwood lumber is again covered by the CVD order from August 6, 2026.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: softwood lumber exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% duties on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. They do not apply to Section 232 softwood lumber (note 52(f)(4)), tropical logs, lumber and veneer are on the general exemption list (note 52(b)), and 11 partners have exception lists covering tropical plywood and flooring (note 52(j)). They reach up to 419 Chapter 44 lines: plywood, MDF, OSB, pellets, mouldings, doors, windows, flooring and most articles. USMCA goods are exempt.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It did not apply in addition to Section 232 duties (Proclamation 11012), so softwood lumber paid only its 10%; other wood products paid it unless USMCA goods or on its exemption list (9903.03.03).

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil: lumber and tropical wood exempt, plywood not
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Section 232 softwood lumber is excluded (note 50(a)(vi)(4)) and tropical logs, lumber, veneer, flooring strips and tropical plywood are on the exemption list (note 50(a)(ii)); it reaches 350 Chapter 44 lines, including Brazilian pine plywood, MDF, mouldings and doors.

changes.title: Wood mouldings and millwork orders on China continued
changes.detail: After sunset reviews, Commerce continued the 2021 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on wood mouldings and millwork products from China (mainly 4409.10, 4409.22, 4409.29 and some 4418).

changes.title: Softwood lumber: preliminary results of the 2024 reviews
changes.detail: Commerce published preliminary results of the 2024 antidumping and countervailing duty administrative reviews of Canadian softwood lumber. Cash-deposit rates change only when the final results are published; until then the rates from the 2023 reviews apply (35.19% for most producers).

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Proclamation 11012 says it does not apply in addition to Section 232 duties, so softwood lumber paid only 10%; USMCA goods were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026. The Section 232 lumber duty is not an IEEPA duty and continued.

changes.title: Furniture and cabinet steps delayed to 2027; lumber unchanged
changes.detail: Proclamation 11000 moved the scheduled increases on upholstered wooden furniture (25% to 30%) and kitchen cabinets and vanities (25% to 50%) from January 1, 2026 to January 1, 2027. Those goods are in Chapter 94; the 10% duty on softwood lumber did not change.

changes.title: Section 232 timber and lumber duty: 10% on softwood
changes.detail: Proclamation 10976 imposed a 10% duty on softwood timber and lumber (9903.76.01) from every country from October 14, 2025, with 25% on upholstered wooden furniture and kitchen cabinets and vanities (Chapter 94). The UK's lumber duty is capped at 10% and the EU's and Japan's total at 15%. Wood products that pay the Section 232 auto duties pay those instead.

changes.title: Softwood lumber CVD: 14.63% for most Canadian producers
changes.detail: Final results of the 2023 countervailing duty review: Canfor 12.12%, West Fraser 16.82%, non-selected companies 14.63%. These became the cash-deposit rates for new entries.

changes.title: Softwood lumber AD: 20.56% for most Canadian producers
changes.detail: Final results of the 2023 antidumping duty review: Canfor 35.53%, West Fraser 9.65%, non-selected companies 20.56%. With the CVD, most Canadian producers pay 35.19% in AD/CVD cash deposits, on top of the 10% Section 232 duty since October 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariffs (ended)
changes.detail: Executive Order 14257 set reciprocal tariffs on goods of most countries from April 5, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026, with the other IEEPA tariffs.

changes.title: IEEPA duty on Canada (ended)
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) from March 4, 2025; USMCA goods were exempted from March 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Multilayered wood flooring orders on China continued
changes.detail: Commerce continued the 2011 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on multilayered wood flooring from China (4412 and 4418.7x engineered flooring).

changes.title: Hardwood plywood orders on China continued
changes.detail: Commerce continued the 2018 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on certain hardwood plywood products from China.

changes.title: Russian wood: 35% in lieu of column 2
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 raised the duty on listed Russian products, including wood products, to 35% in place of the column 2 rate (9903.90.08) from July 27, 2022; Proclamation 10523 added more Russian goods in 2023.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 covers most wood products
changes.detail: USTR's third list (9903.88.03) put 10%, raised to 25% in May 2019, on most Chinese Chapter 44 products, including lumber, plywood, flooring and mouldings.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 44 wood were **$23.21B in 2025**, -5.3% from $24.51B in 2024 (peak: $36.29B in 2022, when lumber prices were high). The five largest suppliers were Canada ($10.16B, 44%), China ($1.61B), Brazil ($1.48B), Vietnam ($1.38B) and Chile ($1.14B). By product group the largest were sawn lumber (4407, $7.44B), plywood and laminated wood (4412, $3.52B), builders' joinery (4418, $3.05B) and particle board and OSB (4410, $2.00B). S-P-F softwood lumber (4407.13) alone was 17% of the chapter.

Canada fell 12.3% and China 25.8% in 2025, while Vietnam (+24.6%), Indonesia (+21.2%), Sweden (+17.5%) and Germany (+11.9%) grew. The 10% Section 232 duty on softwood lumber started only in October 2025, and Canada's Section 338 duty in August 2026, so their full effect is not yet in annual data.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For **softwood lumber and logs** the answer is the same everywhere: **10%** (Section 232), because the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties do not stack on it. For **other wood products** the country matters: Canadian plywood, hardwood lumber, MDF and windows pay **50%** (Section 338, even with USMCA), China pays **25% plus 12.5%** on most lines, Brazil 25% plus 12.5%, and most other suppliers their base rate plus 10% or 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 actions (EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan: 10% or 12.5% in place of the base rate). Tropical logs, lumber and veneer are exempt from the 2026 actions.

The table does **not** include antidumping or countervailing duties: Canadian softwood lumber (35.19% for most producers), Chinese hardwood plywood, multilayered flooring and mouldings, and the new hardwood and decorative plywood case on China, Indonesia and Vietnam (see Tariff updates).

Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

seo.title: Importing Lumber & Wood: Lacey Act Declaration, APHIS, ISPM 15, Formaldehyde Certification & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 44) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 44 wood line: Lacey Act declaration, APHIS log and lumber rules, ISPM 15 for pallets, TSCA formaldehyde certification for plywood and MDF, Section 232 lumber entry, AD/CVD scope, plus the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, origin, correct classification and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For wood, the paperwork is about the forest as much as the tariff. Most Chapter 44 entries need a **Lacey Act declaration** naming the genus, species and country of harvest of the wood, logs and lumber must meet **APHIS** pest rules, wood pallets and crates must carry the **ISPM 15** mark, and plywood, particle board and MDF must be **TSCA Title VI** formaldehyde-certified. Softwood lumber is entered with the Section 232 heading 9903.76.01, and Canadian softwood lumber with its AD/CVD case numbers and cash deposits.

The legal ways to pay less: claim USMCA where it still helps (it removes the 2026 Section 301 duty but not Section 232 or Section 338), choose origins outside China and the Section 338 list, classify correctly (softwood vs hardwood, plywood vs LVL or flooring), check AD/CVD scope and company rates before you buy, and use drawback for re-exported goods. Each rule and lever links to its regulation or proclamation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican wood
levers.saves: The base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94) on OSB, particle board, most hardwood lumber, flooring, pellets and other non-Section 232 wood
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada or Mexico on lines that are not Section 232 lumber or on Canada's Section 338 lists
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer (no set format), available to CBP on request.
levers.caveat: A USMCA claim does not reduce the 10% Section 232 duty on softwood lumber, the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian plywood, MDF and other listed goods, or the softwood lumber AD/CVD.

levers.saves: 25% to 37.5% on Chinese wood (Section 301); 50% on Canadian plywood, hardwood lumber, MDF and windows (Section 338)
levers.appliesTo: All lines for China; the 154 Section 338 lines for Canada
levers.document: Origin records showing where the product was made. For Chapter 44, the tariff-shift rules of 19 CFR 102.20 decide origin; ask CBP for a binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Third-country processing does not change the Section 232 rate (10% everywhere) and can fall under AD/CVD circumvention or evasion findings for Chinese plywood and flooring.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20 and 51

levers.title: Classify softwood, hardwood and panels correctly
levers.saves: The 10% Section 232 duty on lines that are not softwood logs or lumber (hardwood and tropical lumber, plywood, OSB, LVL, flooring), or the Section 338 duty on lines that are not listed
levers.document: Species and processing records (coniferous vs non-coniferous; rough, planed or end-jointed; laminated veneer vs plywood; flooring panels) and, if unsure, a CBP binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the product, not the duty: declaring softwood as hardwood, or finished flooring as lumber, is a penalty case and can be Lacey Act false labeling.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 37

levers.title: Use the tropical-wood exemptions
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty (10%–12.5%) and, for Brazil, the 25% Brazil duty on tropical logs, lumber, veneer and tropical-faced plywood
levers.appliesTo: Tropical logs, lumber and veneer on the note 52(b) list (all countries); tropical plywood and flooring on the note 52(j) partner lists (11 partners) and the note 50(a)(ii) Brazil list
levers.document: Species declaration (Lacey Act) and product specifications showing the tropical species and, for plywood, the face ply.
levers.caveat: Each list names specific subheadings; tropical wood classified elsewhere pays the duty. China's Section 301 lists still apply to Chinese tropical wood.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 50(a)(ii), 52(b) and 52(j)

levers.title: Check AD/CVD scope and company rates before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping or countervailing duty, when the product or producer is outside the order, or the gap between company rates (for Canadian lumber 9.65% to 35.53% AD)
levers.appliesTo: Canadian softwood lumber (4407.1x, some 4409 and 4418), Chinese hardwood plywood, multilayered flooring and mouldings, and hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam
levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides) and the producer's company-specific cash-deposit rate; when unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: A product in scope pays the cash deposit even if entered under another HTS line. Rates change with each administrative review; the 2024 lumber review results are preliminary.

levers.title: Drawback for re-exported wood
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the base rate, Section 301, Section 338 and other ordinary duties on goods exported or used in exported products
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: AD/CVD are never refundable (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)). Check the Section 232 proclamation before claiming drawback of the lumber duty.

seo.title: Lumber Tariffs FAQ: Canadian Lumber Duties, 10% Section 232, Plywood, China, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 44) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. lumber and wood tariffs: the tariff on Canadian lumber, the 10% Section 232 duty, softwood lumber AD/CVD rates, plywood tariffs from Canada, China, Vietnam and Brazil, OSB, pellets, and HS codes for wood.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most-searched questions about U.S. tariffs on lumber, plywood and other wood imports, by country, by product and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the detail and the official sources.
keyTakeaways: Softwood logs, sleepers and lumber (106 lines of 4403, 4406 and 4407.1x) pay the 10% Section 232 duty from every country since October 14, 2025, on top of any FTA or USMCA rate; hardwood and tropical lumber, plywood, OSB and other wood products are not covered.

Canadian softwood lumber also pays antidumping and countervailing duties, 35.19% for most producers, so about 45% in total. Canadian plywood, hardwood lumber nesoi, MDF, mouldings and windows pay the 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026, even with USMCA.

Chinese wood pays 25% Section 301 (List 3) plus 12.5% on most non-lumber lines; Brazil 25% + 12.5% on plywood and most articles; most other suppliers their base rate plus 10% or 12.5%. Tropical logs, lumber and veneer are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.
In 2025 the U.S. imported $23.21B of Chapter 44 wood, Canada ($10.16B, 44%) first, then China ($1.61B), Brazil ($1.48B) and Vietnam ($1.38B).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Canadian lumber?
searchedAs: how much is the tariff on canadian lumber
faqs.answer: Canadian softwood lumber (4407.11–4407.19) pays the 10% Section 232 duty (9903.76.01), with or without a USMCA claim, plus antidumping and countervailing duty cash deposits: 20.56% AD and 14.63% CVD for most producers (35.19%), from the 2023 reviews; Canfor and West Fraser have their own rates. That is about 45% in total. Section 338 does not apply to softwood lumber. The 2024 reviews are still preliminary.

faqs.question: What is the Section 232 tariff on lumber, and what does it cover?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on lumber
faqs.answer: Proclamation 10976 put a 10% duty on softwood timber and lumber from every country from October 14, 2025 (heading 9903.76.01): coniferous logs and poles, coniferous sleepers and sawn softwood lumber including S-P-F and hem-fir. Hardwood and tropical lumber, plywood, OSB, MDF and finished wood products are not covered. The same proclamation charges 25% on upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets (Chapter 94); Proclamation 11000 moved their increases to January 1, 2027.

faqs.question: Are lumber tariffs still in effect after the Supreme Court ruling?
searchedAs: are lumber tariffs still in effect
tariffs on wood still in effect
faqs.answer: Yes. The Supreme Court's February 20, 2026 ruling ended only the IEEPA tariffs (stopped February 24, 2026). The 10% lumber duty rests on Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, the softwood lumber AD/CVD on the Tariff Act of 1930, and Canada's Section 338 duty on Section 338 of the Tariff Act; all are in force and in the current tariff schedule (2026 Revision 21).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on plywood, OSB and other wood products from Canada?
faqs.answer: Canadian plywood, hardwood lumber nesoi (4407.99), coniferous veneer, mouldings, MDF, windows and some other articles (154 lines) pay the 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14, 9903.03.12) since August 22, 2026, even with USMCA. OSB, particle board, most hardwood lumber, engineered flooring and pellets are not on the lists and are Free with a USMCA certification (10% without it).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on wood and plywood from China?
faqs.answer: Most Chinese wood products pay their base rate plus 25% (Section 301 List 3) plus 12.5% (2026 Section 301): Chinese plywood at 8% pays 45.5%. Chinese softwood lumber pays 35% (10% Section 232 + 25%). Chinese hardwood plywood is also under AD/CVD orders since 2018, and hardwood and decorative plywood faces a new case (ITC affirmative September 9, 2026); Chinese multilayered flooring and mouldings carry AD/CVD too.

faqs.question: Are there new duties on plywood from Vietnam and Indonesia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Commerce made final affirmative dumping and subsidy findings on hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam on July 21, 2026, and the ITC found injury on September 9, 2026 (softwood structural plywood was excluded as negligible). The orders follow; check the cash-deposit rate for your producer. On top, Vietnamese plywood pays its base rate plus 12.5% and Indonesian plywood base plus 10% (tropical plywood on Indonesia's exception list pays only its base rate).

faqs.question: What are lumber and wood tariffs by country?
faqs.answer: Softwood lumber: 10% from every country (plus AD/CVD for Canada). Other wood products: Canada 50% on the Section 338 lines, Free with USMCA otherwise; China base + 37.5% on most lines; Brazil base + 37.5% on plywood and most articles; Vietnam and Chile base + 12.5%; Indonesia and Cambodia base + 10%; the EU 10% in place of the base rate; Mexico Free with USMCA; Russia 35% in place of the base rate plus 12.5%.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import lumber and wood from?
searchedAs: where does the us import lumber from
how much lumber does the us import from canada
faqs.answer: In 2025 the United States imported $23.21B of Chapter 44 wood. The largest suppliers were Canada ($10.16B), China ($1.61B), Brazil ($1.48B), Vietnam ($1.38B) and Chile ($1.14B). The biggest product groups were sawn lumber (4407, $7.44B), plywood (4412, $3.52B), builders' joinery (4418, $3.05B) and OSB and particle board (4410, $2.00B).

faqs.question: Are there exemptions from the lumber and wood tariffs?
faqs.answer: For Section 232 lumber, no country exemptions: USMCA does not reduce it; the UK is capped at 10% and the EU and Japan at 15%, which the 10% already meets. For other wood, USMCA removes the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican goods (not Section 338), tropical logs, lumber and veneer are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties, 11 partners have exception lists for tropical plywood and flooring, and Brazil's duty exempts tropical wood.

faqs.question: What documents do I need to import lumber or plywood?
searchedAs: how to import lumber into the us
faqs.answer: A Lacey Act declaration (PPQ 505) with the genus, species and country of harvest; APHIS compliance for logs, lumber and chips (treatment or permit conditions by origin); ISPM 15-marked wood packaging; TSCA Title VI formaldehyde certification and labels for hardwood plywood, particle board and MDF; and, for Canadian softwood lumber, the AD/CVD case numbers and cash deposits on the entry.

faqs.question: How are lumber tariffs calculated?
faqs.answer: Add the base rate of the Chapter 44 line (Free for lumber) and the 10% Section 232 duty on the customs value for softwood lumber, plus any duty that stacks: China's 25% Section 301, or for other wood the 2026 Section 301 rate, the Brazil duty or Canada's 50% Section 338 duty. Then add AD/CVD cash deposits for the producer (Canadian softwood lumber, Chinese plywood and flooring). The 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties do not apply on top of Section 232 lumber.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for lumber and wood?
faqs.answer: Wood is HTS Chapter 44: pellets and chips 4401, charcoal 4402, logs 4403, sawn lumber 4407 (softwood 4407.11–4407.19, S-P-F 4407.13), veneer 4408, mouldings and flooring strips 4409, particle board and OSB 4410, MDF and fiberboard 4411, plywood and LVL 4412, pallets 4415, doors, windows, engineered flooring and glulam 4418, kitchenware 4419 and other articles 4421. Furniture and cabinets are in Chapter 94. Use the rate table to search by product name.
